content:
Every December the question returns: may a Muslim say "Merry Christmas" to a Christian neighbour, colleague or relative? One side answers that every scholar has forbidden it. The other answers that no serious scholar ever objected. Both answers are false.

The scholars have disagreed, and their disagreement is on record. Ibn al-Qayyim forbade congratulating others on their religious rites, and Ibn ʿUthaymin applied that to Christmas. The Mufti of the Federal Territories in Malaysia and Egypt's Dar al-Iftaʾ permit the greeting, each with conditions.[1]

This article aims to provide context to the question, insha'Allah, in five positions taken by named scholars and fatwa bodies, with their reasons. Every one of them begins from the same verse: "Allah forbids you not, with regard to those who fight you not for (your) Faith nor drive you out of your homes, from dealing kindly and justly with them: for Allah loveth those who are just" (60:8).[2]

The classical prohibition is stated most sharply by Ibn al-Qayyim (d. 1350) in Aḥkām ahl al-dhimma: "Congratulating the non-Muslims on the rituals that belong only to them is prohibited by consensus."[3] He held it a worse sin than congratulating a man for drinking wine, and the Federal Territories Mufti quotes him in full in its survey of the question.[1]

His concern was the rite itself. A festival that marks a creed is part of that creed, and congratulating its people on it, in his reading, honours what Islam rejects. The Mufti's survey sets him beside other classical jurists who forbade taking part in the festivals of other faiths or congratulating their people on them.[1]

Muḥammad ibn ʿUthaymīn (d. 2001) applied the classical rule directly: "Greeting the non-Muslims on Christmas and other religious holidays of theirs is prohibited by consensus." Islam Q&A reproduces his fatwa with Ibn al-Qayyim's words and those of Ibn Taymiyya.[3]

The Federal Territories Mufti lists Ibn Baz and Muhammad Salih al-Munajjid among the contemporary scholars of this view.[1] They do not forbid kindness to Christians. Their position separates good treatment of people, which 60:8 commands, from a greeting tied to a religious feast, which they hold the verse does not cover.

Many contemporary scholars disagree with the claim of consensus. The Federal Territories Mufti lists among those who permit the greeting Mustafa al-Zarqa, Yusuf al-Qaradawi, Abdullah bin Bayyah, Muhammad Saʿid Ramadan al-Buti, Ali Jumʿa and Ahmad al-Tayyib, Shaykh al-Azhar.[1]

Their reasons differ. Al-Qaradawi rests his view on 60:8. Ibn Bayyah classes the greeting as mujāmala, courteous speech, which acknowledges the people and makes no claim about their faith.[1] On their reading, the words "Merry Christmas" in ordinary use wish a person well, and the speaker's creed is untouched.

Egypt's Dar al-Iftaʾ ruled in 2013: "In Islamic law, there is no objection to congratulating and sharing peaceful non-Muslims their religious occasions". It cites 60:8, and the command on greetings: "When a (courteous) greeting is offered you, meet it with a greeting still more courteous, or (at least) of equal courtesy" (4:86).[4] Congratulating them, it says, does "not necessitate acknowledging their disbelief or corrupt convictions."[4]

A fatwa of December 2024 answered a question on Christmas greetings to Christian friends and family. It allows the Muslim to share their happiness and celebrations, "provided they do not involve any religious rites or practices that contradict Islam."[5] The line Dar al-Iftaʾ draws runs between social courtesy and worship.

Malaysia's National Fatwa Committee ruled at its 78th meeting, on 12 June 2007, that a greeting to non-Muslims on their festivals "adalah harus, dengan syarat ucapan itu tidak mengiktiraf, memuji atau memuliakan agama bukan Muslim": it is permissible, provided the greeting does not recognise, praise or glorify the other religion. It must also use none of that religion's symbols.[6]

The Federal Territories Mufti weighed both sides in 2018 and reached the same answer: "Hukumnya adalah harus dengan meraikan garis panduan yang dinyatakan", the ruling is that it is permissible within the stated guidelines.[6] For Muslims in Malaysia, that is the guidance of their own religious authorities.

Every position above commands kindness and justice to peaceful Christians, on the authority of 60:8. None of them permits a Muslim to affirm the divinity of Jesus, and none of them permits joining in Christian worship. The disagreement is over one question: does a seasonal greeting honour a creed, or does it wish a neighbour well?

The Quran's ruling on the creed is unchanged by either answer: "Christ the son of Mary was no more than a messenger; many were the messengers that passed away before him" (5:75).[2] We set out the Quran's wider guidance on relations with Christians in can a Muslim befriend a non-Muslim?, and the history of the date and the customs in was Jesus born on 25 December? and 6 Christmas traditions and their historical origins.

The bottom line

The scholars of Islam have not spoken with one voice on Christmas greetings. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn ʿUthaymin forbade them as congratulation on a religious rite. Al-Qaradawi, Ibn Bayyah, Dar al-Iftaʾ and Malaysia's National Fatwa Committee permit them as courtesy, on condition that nothing in them affirms another creed or joins its worship.

A Muslim who follows either view follows recognised scholarship, and neither has left Islam by doing so. All of them answer to the same verse on how to treat a peaceful neighbour: "Allah loveth those who are just" (60:8).[2] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Jabatan Mufti Wilayah Persekutuan, "Tahqiq al-Masail 7: Hukum Mengucapkan 'Merry Christmas' kepada Mereka yang Beragama Kristian", 24 December 2018, citing Ibn al-Qayyim, Aḥkām ahl al-dhimma, vol. 1, p. 441.
  2. Quran 4:86; 5:75; 60:8, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Muḥammad ibn ʿUthaymīn and Ibn al-Qayyim, quoted in "Greeting Non-Muslims on Their Festivals", Islam Q&A, answer 947.
  4. Dar al-Iftaʾ al-Misriyya, "Permissibility of Congratulating Non-Muslims on Their Religious Festivals", fatwa 6710, 18 November 2013.
  5. Dar al-Iftaʾ al-Misriyya, "Congratulating Non-Muslims on Christmas", fatwa 21593, 2 December 2024.
  6. Jabatan Mufti Wilayah Persekutuan, "Tinta Mufti Bil. 47/2025: Garis Panduan dan Hukum-Hakam Berkaitan Penglibatan Muslim dalam Perayaan Krismas", 18 December 2025, citing the 78th Muzakarah of the National Fatwa Committee, 12 June 2007.
